column4: The section glosses the roots of al-yusr and al-‘usr as financial plenty and want; here the debtor is actually in ‘usr and is given time until maysara, with charity better still. This is the clearest lived case of the section’s purse moving from shortage toward abundance.

The section reads al-yusr and al-‘usr through wealth and want; this verse explicitly joins spending according to one’s sa‘a (means) to Allah making ease after ‘usr, showing both its financial and ordinary sense.

The section links b-kh-l (withholding possessions) with gh-n-y (self-sufficiency). This verse joins the same root b-kh-l to “Allah is al-Ghani and you are poor,” overturning the miser’s claim to sufficiency.
The section’s source word istaghna in 92:8 means that a person sees himself as self-sufficient; 96:6 says the human being transgresses, setting up the consequence of that stance.
The section’s source word istaghna in 92:8 means seeing oneself as sufficient; this verse names precisely that trigger, “when he sees himself as self-sufficient” (ra’ahu istaghna).
The section cites this exact istaghna form for the person who considers himself sufficient, in contrast to the miser’s path in 92:8; here the Prophet is drawn toward the self-satisfied visitor.
The section says the self-sufficient man receives attention; this is the rebuke’s next detail, “you attend to him” (tasadda), while the blind seeker is neglected in the surrounding passage.
The section describes attention given to the self-sufficient man; this verse says the Prophet is not accountable if that man does not purify himself, clarifying the misplaced priority in the rebuke.
The section reads ease and hardship as abundance and lack. Here a person interprets expanded provision as proof that God honored him; the following verses expose that inference as false.

The section’s financial reading of ease and hardship meets this verse’s restricted provision, which the person wrongly treats as humiliation. Its own claim supplies the scarcity side of that mistaken equation.
After the rich person’s mistaken inference, this verse says they do not honor the orphan; abundance has not made the holder generous, directly exposing the section’s b-kh-l pattern.
This verse says they do not urge feeding the poor. It gives a concrete human cost for the section’s image of holding acquired wealth instead of letting it benefit others.
The section glosses wealth as acquired possessions and stinginess as keeping them back; this verse depicts devouring inheritance greedily, a particularly direct form of grasping at property.
The section’s image of a man rich in possessions who sees himself as sufficient is sharpened here by the claim that people love wealth with an intense love.
Qarun is given treasures so abundant that their keys burden a group of strong men. This makes the section’s full purse concrete before the story shows what that wealth can and cannot do.
The section’s istaghna describes imagined self-sufficiency; Qarun says his wealth was given because of knowledge he possesses, presenting the same claim of standing secure through oneself.
Qarun comes before his people in his adornment, and those who desire worldly life wish for his position. This shows wealth’s public power before the section’s warning that it cannot secure its owner.

The knowledgeable observers say God’s reward is better for the one who believes and acts well. Their response sets durable worth against the wealth and display that attract the crowd in the preceding verse.
The earth swallows Qarun and his house, and he has no group to help him. This is a precise reversal of the rich man’s apparent security: his property and status cannot protect him.

After Qarun’s fall, the people who wanted his position recognize that God expands and restricts provision as He wills. This directly joins the section’s wealth-and-want reading to the collapse of presumed self-sufficiency.
The owner of the two gardens boasts that he has more wealth and stronger support. His boast stages the section’s rich man who feels secure because of what he owns.

The garden owner says he does not think the Hour will come and expects something better if returned; this is self-sufficiency extended into a false promise of permanence, like the section’s warning about wealth at death.
After his gardens are ruined, the owner wrings his hands over what he spent. The scene makes visible the section’s claim that accumulated wealth can slip away and leave its owner helpless.
The garden owner has no group to help him against God. This is the story’s explicit answer to the security implied by his wealth and status.
The story concludes that true protection belongs to God, the Real; this supplies the source of lasting help after the wealthy owner’s possessions and human backing fail.

The section names fear of poverty as the pressure behind holding wealth back; this verse explicitly says Satan promises poverty while Allah promises forgiveness and bounty, revealing the competing voices around giving.

The section notes that the next surah says Allah found the Prophet in need and enriched him (a’ila fa-agna). It makes sufficiency a gift from God rather than an achievement secured by hoarded property.

At death, a person asks for a brief delay so he can give charity (fa-assaddaqa). This directly matches the section’s scene of wealth no longer helping at the fall and the dying person wishing he had given.

The section says the giver seeks God’s face and expects no repayment from anyone; here the people who feed others say they want from them neither recompense nor thanks (la nuridu minkum jaz’an wa la shukura).

The section says the giver does not give to settle a debt or receive recompense; this command warns against giving in order to get more in return (wa la تمنن تستكثر), a direct boundary on transactional generosity.

The section says the generous person owes no human a return and gives seeking God’s face. This verse says spending is for oneself and is done seeking Allah’s face; what is spent is repaid fully by God.

The section contrasts withholding with giving that seeks no human repayment; this verse describes spenders who do not follow their gift with reminders or injury, so the recipient is not made indebted to the giver.

The section opposes b-kh-l to generosity and glosses ghani as wealth and sufficiency; this verse says kind speech and pardon are better than hurtful charity, then calls Allah al-Ghani, joining generous conduct to true sufficiency.
This verse praises those who spend in both ease and hardship. The section gives those same ease and hardship roots a financial sense, so the verse shows generosity across both fullness and want.

The section names stinginess as holding possessions back and generosity as its opposite; this verse describes spending without extravagance or miserliness, giving a measured practice between closed and emptied hands.

The section evokes the purse becoming full or empty and defines b-kh-l as holding possessions back; this verse pictures a hand neither chained to the neck nor extended completely, with destitution as the consequence of excess.
This verse describes giving wealth, despite love of it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler, alongside patience in hardship. It makes the section’s alternative to hoarding concrete.
The section contrasts holding wealth with giving for God’s sake; this verse says righteousness is not attained until one spends from what one loves, directly testing attachment to acquired property.

The section describes the wealthy miser as holding acquired possessions back; this verse says that if people owned the treasuries of their Lord’s mercy they would still withhold for fear of spending, naming the fear beneath grasping.

The section’s b-kh-l means holding possessions back when they should be released; this verse describes those who withhold what Allah gave them, mistaking it for good, and says what they withheld will burden them on the Day of Resurrection.
The section defines b-kh-l as keeping acquired property from where it should go; this verse names those who are stingy, urge others to stinginess, and conceal Allah’s bounty.
After receiving bounty, the people in this verse become miserly with it and turn away. This is the section’s movement from provision to withholding in an explicit narrative.
The section’s image centers on b-kh-l and presumed self-sufficiency; this verse names the stingy person who commands stinginess and says Allah is al-Ghani, worthy of praise.

The section defines withholding as keeping possessions from their proper recipient; this verse says there is a recognized right in wealth for the asker and deprived person, the direct claim that wealth is not only for its holder.
The section frames wealth as possessions that can be held or released; this verse says the steadfast worshippers reserve a recognized share of their wealth for others.
This verse identifies the recipients of that share as the asker and the deprived, giving a concrete opposite to the section’s miser who keeps wealth back.

The section presents b-kh-l as the miser’s path; this verse praises people who prefer others over themselves even when they themselves are in need and says those protected from their own avarice succeed.
This verse commands spending and says whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul succeeds, directly naming the inward counterpart of the section’s b-kh-l.

This verse commands spending from the good things people have earned. The section glosses mal as acquired property and depicts the miser keeping possessions back, so this names what should be released.
This verse distinguishes wealth given to increase through people’s property from charity seeking God’s face; it clarifies the section’s giver who expects no payment from a human recipient.
This verse says what people spend is replaced by God. That offers a specific counterpart to the section’s giver, who seeks God’s face rather than asking a person to repay him.
The section says the roots y-s-r and ‘-s-r can name abundance and lack; in the fasting rule here they mean ease and hardship in observance, showing the same pair in a nonfinancial sense.
The section reads the ‘-s-r/y-s-r pair financially; this verse uses ‘usr for difficulty and yusr for ease in the repeated promise that ease accompanies hardship, without making the subject money.
This repeats the section’s named ‘-s-r/y-s-r roots in the ordinary sense of hardship and ease. The repetition strengthens the other, financial sense developed in the section.
The section names al-yusra in 92:7 and traces it to y-s-r; here Allah says He will ease the Prophet toward al-yusra, a close wording in a different, nonfinancial setting.

After 2:280 allows time for a debtor in hardship and recommends charity, this neighboring verse warns of the Day when every soul is repaid in full. Its contribution is the final accounting that makes present wealth and generosity matter.

This is the frown and turning away that begins the passage cited by the section; the following verses identify the visitor as blind, so this row opens the scene in which attention shifts toward the self-sufficient man.
This verse identifies the visitor as the blind man, completing the scene behind the section’s contrast between the man who sees himself as sufficient and the seeker who came for guidance.
The rebuke asks what could make the Prophet know that the blind visitor might be purified. It explains why the neglected seeker mattered in the scene cited by the section.
The verse says the blind visitor might receive a reminder and benefit; it shows the value of the seeker whom the self-satisfied visitor displaced.
The passage turns from the self-satisfied man to one who comes striving; this neighboring contrast gives the neglected seeker’s own approach.
The seeker is described as fearing God, completing the contrast with the man who considers himself self-sufficient in the section’s cited passage.
The passage says the Prophet is distracted from this God-fearing seeker. It completes the rebuke’s reversal of attention around self-sufficiency and need.
The section cites 111:2’s statement that Abu Lahab’s wealth and earnings did not avail him; this next verse names the blazing fire he will enter, giving the failure its immediate consequence.
After the speaker says in 69:28 that his wealth did not avail him, this verse says his authority has perished too. It completes the loss of the resources he might have counted on.
This verse describes gathering wealth and counting it; the next verse says the collector imagines his wealth will make him immortal, the exact false security the section sets beside death.
After 104:2-3 depicts wealth amassed and imagined to grant permanence, this verse says the person will be cast into al-Hutama, showing the limit of that imagined security.
After 26:88 says wealth and sons do not benefit on that Day, this verse names the sound heart as the exception, specifying what has value when possessions fail.
After the dying person asks in 63:10 for time to give charity, this neighboring verse says Allah will not delay a soul when its term arrives. It closes the scene of too-late regret.
This verse describes religious leaders who hoard gold and silver instead of spending in God’s way; it is a concrete form of the section’s miserly holding of possessions.
The next verse depicts that hoarded gold and silver heated and used to brand their foreheads, sides, and backs. It shows the hoarder’s wealth becoming punishment rather than protection.
The next verse says a barrier lies behind the dead until resurrection. It completes the return-request scene by closing the chance to act again.

The verse names the stupor of death arriving with truth. The section’s dictionary explicitly gives death-swoon as a secondary sense of the root behind 92:1’s covering, and places the loss of wealth at that threshold.
This verse stages the soul reaching the throat while onlookers watch; it gives bodily form to the death threshold at which the section says possessions slip from their owner.
The verse describes the onlookers standing nearby as the soul reaches the throat, completing the helpless scene at which the section’s wealth can no longer suffice.
The verse says Allah is nearer to the dying person than the observers, though they do not perceive it. This places divine reality beyond the visible wealth left around the deathbed.
The passage concludes by challenging the onlookers to bring the soul back if they are truthful; this completes the helpless death scene behind the section’s image of wealth dropping away.
This verse stages the death moment as the soul reaching the collarbones. The section’s dictionary connects 92:1’s covering root to death-swoon, and says the owner’s wealth fails at that threshold.
As the death scene continues, those present ask who can heal the dying person. This shows the limit of human help at the point where the section says possessions can no longer suffice.
The dying person recognizes that this is departure, completing the scene of the section’s death threshold where held wealth slips away.
The verse describes the legs being joined together as death approaches; it continues the bodily scene of the final moment that the section associates with loss of possessions.
The passage ends with the person being driven to his Lord. This completes the death scene and turns from possessions that cannot help to the reckoning that follows.

The section develops yaghsha in 92:1 as night covering a person, with a dictionary sense extending to death-swoon; 91:4 repeats the night-covering scene (yaghshaha), though its referent is the celestial body in the surrounding oath.
The section names the root gh-sh-w for covering and gives death-swoon as a secondary sense; here the sea covers Pharaoh’s people in a fatal scene, a concrete lethal form of that covering.

The section develops the root gh-sh-w as covering and links it to death-swoon; here waves cover people like canopies and they call to God in helplessness, a parallel of exposure to what overwhelms them.

The section’s j-z-y gloss includes the claim that a parent cannot make up for a child; this verse says no soul will be recompensed for another and no ransom or intercession will be accepted, bounding what wealth or kin can do.
This repeats the section’s j-z-y idea that one person cannot settle another’s account: no soul can avail another, and ransom will not be accepted on that Day.
This verse says wealth and children will not avail the disbelievers against God and that they face the Fire, echoing the section’s boundary on material sufficiency.
The verse repeats that neither wealth nor children avail those who disbelieve, then names the Fire as their end; it is another direct formulation of the section’s warning.
This verse says neither wealth nor children will avail against God and names their owners as companions of the Fire, a direct parallel to the section’s limit on wealth.
The verse says kin and children will not benefit on the Day of Resurrection and that God sees what people do. It extends the section’s boundary from wealth to family ties.
The people claim that their greater wealth and children will spare them from punishment. This is a specific claim of material security that 34:37 directly answers.
This verse says Allah expands and restricts provision as He wills. It gives the section’s abundance-and-lack image a direct statement that provision is not controlled by the wealthy person.

The verse says wealth and children do not bring people near to God, except faith and righteous action. It directly denies that possessions create the sufficiency the section attributes to the miser’s self-image.
This verse warns believers not to let wealth and children distract them from remembering Allah, because those who do are losers. It shows wealth failing as a guide to what matters.
The verse depicts poor people constrained in God’s way who seem self-sufficient because they do not beg insistently. It complicates the section’s equation of visible abundance with actual need.

This verse says Allah expands and restricts provision, while people rejoice in worldly life. It joins the section’s financial reading of plenty and want to the warning that worldly abundance is limited.
This verse says the Lord expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it. It makes financial plenty and shortage dependent on God rather than the holder’s self-sufficiency.
The verse says people are the poor toward Allah and Allah is al-Ghani. This repeats the section’s contrast between human need and the true source of sufficiency.
This verse calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life and says enduring good deeds are better. It gives a specific account of what lasts after the section’s possessions have failed.

This verse describes worldly life as rivalry in increase of wealth and children, then as growth that withers and becomes debris. The passing sequence illuminates the section’s image of possessions slipping away.

After hardship is removed and blessing arrives, the person says “this is mine” and doubts the Hour. This is a specific case of ease becoming an assertion of security, like the section’s self-sufficient man.
This verse says the human being is distressed when touched by hardship; it supplies the shortage side of the next verse’s response to abundance.
The next verse says that when good reaches the human being, he withholds (manu‘a). It directly joins prosperity to the grasping conduct developed in the section.
The section explicitly compares 92:11 with this sentence about Abu Lahab: his wealth did not avail him (ma aghna ‘anhu maluhu). The wording makes the failure of material sufficiency unmistakable.
The section quotes this exact lament by the person given his record in his left hand: “my wealth did not avail me” (ma aghna ‘anni maliyah), a direct boundary on what possessions can save.
The section names the belief that wealth can secure permanence; this verse says the collector imagines his wealth will make him immortal (akhla-dahu), exposing that false sufficiency.
The section invokes Abraham’s prayer for the Day when neither wealth nor sons benefit (la yanfa‘u malun wa la banun). This is the direct limit on the assets the miser counts on.

The section says wealth cannot help at death; this verse says God means to punish disbelievers through their wealth and children in worldly life, while their souls depart in disbelief, reversing their apparent advantage.

This verse similarly says God means to punish disbelievers through their wealth and children in worldly life, not grant security through them, giving the section’s insufficiency claim a sharp reversal.
The section’s image has property falling from its owner at death; here people arrive alone, having left what God provided behind, and their intercessors have disappeared.
The section says the miser’s money cannot help once he falls; this verse gives the dying person’s plea to return and act, a final boundary on the time left for giving.
At the moment the soul reaches the throat, this verse challenges the living to return it if they can. Its context makes explicit the helplessness behind the section’s deathbed image.
